title: Hilbert space connectivity in non-Hermitian many-body systems: emergent scale-dependent amplification and constraint-induced skin localization
authors: Zichang Hao, Wen-Tan Xue, Ching Hua Lee
abstract: Various exotic many-body phenomena such as quantum scars and fractons have been linked to Hilbert space fragmentation. In this work, we find that in non-Hermitian settings, Hilbert space connectivity has an even more universal and fundamental influence, tightly controlling the nature of spectral amplification and state localization. Far more complicated than real-space lattices, non-Hermitian many-body Hilbert space graphs not only possess intricate competing amplification channels, but also global feedback loops connecting remote Fock states related by particle symmetry. These features lead to amplification behavior with unconventional scaling and localization properties. Particle occupation constraints can furthermore remove selected Hilbert space pathways, leading to robust unipolar and asymmetric bipolar skin localization in otherwise reciprocal processes. These results extend beyond simple interacting bosonic models and establish Hilbert space connectivity as a versatile control knob for many-body non-Hermitian critical transitions.
summary: This work reveals that in non-Hermitian many-body systems, the topology of the Hilbert space connectivity graph is a primary determinant of physical behavior. Specifically, particle occupancy constraints act as crucial bottlenecks, inducing robust, directional localization and controlling the rate of spectral amplification. This establishes connectivity as a versatile control knob for non-Hermitian critical transitions.
main_problem: The paper investigates how Hilbert space connectivity fundamentally controls spectral amplification and state localization in non-Hermitian many-body systems.
main_result: The connectivity graph structure, particularly when constrained by particle occupancy, dictates the emergence of robust, size-dependent spectral amplification and specific localization patterns (unipolar/bipolar).
method: The analysis involves constructing and analyzing the Hilbert space connectivity graph, calculating eigenenergy spectra, and comparing results under different boundary conditions and occupancy constraints.
model_or_system: The study uses a minimal 1D bosonic model Hamiltonian involving correlated two-body hoppings, analyzed for $n=2, 3, 4$ particles, exhibiting non-Hermitian dynamics.
key_observables: Spectral amplification ($\max 	ext{Im}(E)$), Hilbert space connectivity graph structure, and localization patterns (unipolar, asymmetric bipolar) quantified by average polarization weight ($ ar{P}_{	ext{pol}}$).
important_parameters: Boson number ($n$), system size ($N$), and the occupancy constraint ($n_{	ext{max\_occ}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing systems with and without the occupancy constraint, and uses the average center-of-mass position as a diagnostic for localization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the connectivity graphs for different particle numbers and boundary conditions, and show localization patterns (e.g., unipolar/bipolar) induced by the occupancy constraint, contrasting them with unconstrained cases.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the role of connectivity in generating spectral transitions (2-boson case), then detailing how bosonic symmetry creates global loops, and finally demonstrating that occupancy constraints are necessary to induce robust, directional localization patterns.
why_interesting: The direct link drawn between the abstract mathematical structure of the Hilbert space graph (connectivity) and observable physical phenomena like spectral amplification and localization makes it highly relevant for understanding non-Hermitian physics in condensed matter.
